section_title: Who is the rider called Faithful and True?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 11 Then I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war. 12 He has eyes like blazing fire, and many royal crowns on His head. He has a name written on Him that only He Himself knows. 13 He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God.

14 The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and pure, follow Him on white horses. 15 And from His mouth proceeds a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and He will rule them with an iron scepter. He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. 16 And He has a name written on His robe and on His thigh: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.

context_lines: Heaven stands open, and John sees a rider on a white horse. His names identify Him: Faithful and True, the Word of God, and King of kings and Lord of lords. This is Christ, coming as the righteous judge. The many royal crowns express His authority above the rulers who have opposed Him.

The blazing eyes recall the vision of Jesus in chapter 1. His robe is dipped in blood, and armies in pure white linen follow Him. John also mentions a name known only to the rider. The vision reveals who He is while leaving that name unexplained.

The sharp sword comes from His mouth. The Greek word rhomphaia refers to a large sword, as [Thayer’s entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/4501.htm) explains. Here its location matters: the picture connects His judgment with what He speaks. The armies follow, while the action of striking the nations and treading the winepress is assigned to Him.

The iron scepter and winepress draw on earlier biblical pictures of royal authority and judgment. The passage brings those images together around one person. The powers that demanded allegiance in earlier chapters now face the One whose right to rule exceeds their own.
common_interpretation_lines: These readings agree that the rider is Christ and that His victory rests on His authority. They differ over how the vision relates to His return. [Walvoord](https://swartzentrover.com/cotor/E-Books/holiness/Walvoord/Revelation/Rev_19.htm) reads it as Christ’s future return to earth. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/19.htm) instead understands this scene as Christ overcoming opposition through His power and the spread of His gospel, before the final judgment. Gill does not take the heavenly armies here to mean glorified believers returning from heaven.

The blood on the robe has more than one proposed explanation. Gill mentions Christ’s own blood, the blood of His persecuted people, and the blood of His enemies, preferring the last. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) also connects it with conquered enemies through Isaiah 63. The verse names the bloodied robe without directly identifying whose blood it is.

Readers also differ about the accompanying armies. Gill identifies believers; Walvoord includes saints and angels. The clothing recalls the bride’s linen in verse 8, but this passage does not give a complete list of everyone in the armies. In either reading, Christ is the central figure who judges and wins.
god_plan_lines: The ruler promised in [Isaiah 11:1–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/11.htm) judges the poor with righteousness and defeats the wicked by the breath of His lips. [Psalm 2:1–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/2.htm) describes rebellious kings confronting God’s appointed King, who receives the nations and an iron scepter. Revelation places those promises around Jesus. His rule brings the world’s competing claims to authority before God’s judgment.

The title Word of God also recalls [John 1:1–5](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/1.htm), where the Word is with God, is God and is the One through whom all things were made. The One who judges creation is already connected with its beginning.

The bloodied clothing and winepress recall the divine warrior in [Isaiah 63:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/63.htm), where judgment and redemption belong to the same scene. That is a supported connection in the imagery. A detailed route for Christ’s return would require further interpretation beyond what John gives here.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
